title: Cases: where, when, what
description: Six children to work through from the history and examination to a level, a tempo and a differential, each followed by the attending's debrief.
why: A method of localization earns its place only when it works on the child in front of you, taken in order from where to when to what.
objectives: Work a case in order: choose the high-yield examination, commit to a level, then a tempo, then a differential.
Name the one sign that clinches each localization and the trap that most often derails it.
Present a case in where, when, what form.

sections.title: Case 1: a 6-year-old who has stopped walking
sections.content:
**Where.** The examination that matters most here takes about a minute, and it is the reflexes. They are absent everywhere, and areflexia moves the lesion out of the brain and spinal cord and into the motor unit. The distal tingling then rules out the horn cell, the junction and the muscle, which are all purely motor, and leaves the nerves and roots. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a polyradiculoneuropathy, so if you chose nerve or root, you were right. The weakness on both sides of the face does not mean a second lesion. The facial nerves are peripheral nerves, and the same process can reach them.

**When.** The weakness has climbed over four days, beginning two weeks after an infection. A course measured in hours to days points to an immune or inflammatory cause.

**What.** Guillain-Barré is the diagnosis, but the list has to protect two others. Tick paralysis looks the same and is cured by finding the tick. A cord lesion can also look the same in its first days, because an acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion produces spinal shock, a flaccid, areflexic paralysis (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). Here the search for a sensory level found none and the bladder was normal, and those two findings kept the localization in the nerves and roots.

**The trap.** This case has two traps. The first is calling a child who "won't walk" behavioral before anyone has picked up the reflex hammer, since absent reflexes cannot be produced on purpose. The second concerns the breathing count. It did nothing to help you localize, but it is the examination you will repeat every few hours, because in Guillain-Barré the danger lies with the diaphragm and the autonomic nervous system rather than with the legs.

In where, when, what form: "Peripheral nerve and root, acute over days after an infection, most likely Guillain-Barré syndrome, with tick paralysis and an early cord lesion excluded at the bedside."
keyPoints: Generalized areflexia places the lesion in the motor unit, and distal sensory symptoms narrow it to nerve and root.
A cord lesion can be flaccid and areflexic in its first days (spinal shock), so look for a sensory level and check the bladder (DeMyer, pp. 273-274).
Tick paralysis mimics Guillain-Barré and is cured by removing the tick.
Breathing and autonomic function need serial monitoring, because the danger in Guillain-Barré lies there rather than in the leg weakness.

question.question: On day three of admission the same boy's single-breath count has fallen steadily and his voice is softer. His leg strength is unchanged. What does this change mean?
options: Nothing, because his legs are stable
His respiratory and bulbar muscles are now involved, and he needs urgent assessment for respiratory support
The diagnosis is wrong and he has myasthenia gravis
He is anxious, which explains the change
question.explanation: In Guillain-Barré syndrome the weakness can spread to the diaphragm and the bulbar muscles while the legs look stable, and a falling breath count with a softening voice is the warning that it has. It calls for urgent assessment of respiratory function and a plan for support, and reassurance would be the wrong response, because stable legs do not mean a stable illness. Bulbar and respiratory involvement is part of Guillain-Barré and does not on its own change the diagnosis to myasthenia. Anxiety does not make a measured breath count fall steadily over days.

sections.title: Case 2: a 3-month-old who stopped feeding well
sections.content:
**Where.** In an infant who cannot tell you anything, the examination you choose decides the localization. Ptosis that worsens as you examine, a suck that fades after a few seconds and a cry that weakens are fatigable bulbar and ocular weakness. That pattern is the signature of the neuromuscular junction. The other great cause of a weak, alert, floppy infant is spinal muscular atrophy, and two findings argue against it here. Her tongue has no fasciculations, and her eyelids and eye movements are weak, whereas spinal muscular atrophy spares the eye muscles.

**When.** The course is measured in days, and a week ago this baby held her head well. The problem is therefore neither congenital nor static, which moves congenital myasthenic syndromes and cerebral palsy to the bottom of the list.

**What.** Infant botulism should be suspected in an infant under 6 months with constipation, listlessness, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)), and this baby has exactly that presentation. The constipation belongs to the same story, since the toxin blocks acetylcholine release in the gut as well as at the muscle. Central causes still account for most hypotonia in infants ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). Sepsis and metabolic crises therefore stay on the list in parallel, and a floppy baby who is feeding poorly is treated as a sick baby from the start.

**The trap.** The commonest mistake is to call the hypotonia central simply because central hypotonia is common. Central hypotonia comes with a depressed level of consciousness, axial more than limb weakness, and normal or brisk reflexes ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). This baby is awake and following faces, with weakness that fatigues. The level of alertness is the single most useful fork in the floppy infant, and here it points to the periphery.

Where, when, what: "Neuromuscular junction, acute over days in a previously normal infant, most likely infant botulism, with sepsis and metabolic crisis excluded in parallel."
keyPoints: Fatigable ptosis, a fading suck and a weakening cry localize to the neuromuscular junction.
The absence of tongue fasciculations, and weakness of the eyelids and eye movements, argue against spinal muscular atrophy.
Suspect infant botulism under 6 months with constipation, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag (Peredo 2009).
In the floppy infant the level of alertness is the first fork, and an alert baby with real weakness points to the periphery.

question.question: Which single finding in this baby most strongly separated a peripheral cause from the commoner central causes of infant hypotonia?
options: The constipation
The soft fontanelle
That she was alert and following faces while genuinely weak and fatiguing
The absence of a rash
question.explanation: Central hypotonia typically comes with a depressed level of consciousness, axial weakness and preserved or brisk reflexes. An alert infant who follows faces but has real, fatigable weakness points to the motor unit, which is why the level of alertness is the first fork in the floppy infant. Constipation was a strong clue to botulism once the junction was suspected, but on its own it does not separate central from peripheral causes. A soft fontanelle and the absence of a rash are reassuring, but neither helps to localize.

sections.title: Case 3: a 4-year-old boy who climbs up his own legs
sections.content:
**Where.** You probably had the localization before you touched him, because watching a child get up from the floor is the most efficient examination in pediatric neuromuscular medicine. A Gowers maneuver means proximal hip weakness. Add symmetric girdle weakness, normal sensation and no fasciculations, and the motor unit narrows to muscle or the anterior horn cell. The calves decide between the two, since calf enlargement, lumbar lordosis, a waddling gait and toe walking together point to a dystrophy (Brazis 2011, p. 13).

**When.** The course runs over months to years and has to be read through development. He walked late and has fallen steadily further behind his friends without ever losing a skill. In a toddler, slow progression of this kind often looks like a developmental delay that is not catching up.

**What.** Duchenne muscular dystrophy heads the list, with Becker, its milder relative, beside it. The maternal uncle who needed a wheelchair as a teenager suggests an X-linked pattern, which supports what the examination found. Spinal muscular atrophy also produces proximal weakness and a Gowers sign, so it stays on the list until the creatine kinase level, which is very high in Duchenne, answers the question.

**The trap.** Toe walking nearly sent this boy to orthopedics. It is also a feature of spastic diplegia and of idiopathic toe walking (DeMyer, p. 338), and the rest of the examination decides among them. Brisk reflexes and increased tone point to the upper motor neuron, a Gowers maneuver and big calves point to muscle, and only a completely normal examination allows the idiopathic label. A second trap is ordering the creatine kinase as an afterthought. In a boy who walks late and falls, it is a simple test that can save a long diagnostic journey.

Where, when, what: "Muscle, chronic since early childhood, most likely a dystrophinopathy, so check creatine kinase and then dystrophin genetics." See the [Neuromuscular section](/neuromuscular).
keyPoints: A Gowers maneuver means proximal hip weakness, so watch every weak child get up from the floor.
Calf enlargement, lordosis, waddling and toe walking point to a dystrophy (Brazis 2011, p. 13).
Toe walking has several causes, and the rest of the examination decides between muscle, upper motor neuron and idiopathic (DeMyer, p. 338).
In a boy who walks late and falls, check the creatine kinase early.

question.question: Another 4-year-old boy walks on his toes. He gets up from the floor without using his hands, his knee reflexes are brisk with a few beats of ankle clonus, and his calves are slim. Where is the problem most likely to be?
options: Upper motor neuron, as in spastic diplegia, because toe walking comes with brisk reflexes and clonus rather than proximal weakness
Muscle, because he walks on his toes
Peripheral nerve, because the calves are slim
Nowhere, because this is idiopathic toe walking
question.explanation: Toe walking is a sign with several addresses. This boy has no Gowers maneuver and therefore no proximal weakness, while his brisk reflexes and clonus point to the upper motor neuron, as in spastic diplegia. Choosing muscle rests on the toe walking alone and ignores the reflexes. A neuropathy would lower the reflexes rather than make them brisk, and idiopathic toe walking requires an otherwise normal examination, which brisk reflexes with clonus rule out.

sections.title: Case 4: a 13-year-old whose legs went numb from the waist down
sections.content:
**Where.** Weak legs could come from many places, and the reduced reflexes might have tempted you toward the periphery. A sensory level on the trunk, though, almost always means the cord (Brazis 2011, p. 104), and early urinary retention agrees with it. The upgoing toes settle the matter. They show that the reflexes are reduced by spinal shock from an acute, severe lesion of the cord rather than by a peripheral lesion (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). As she recovers from the spinal shock, her reflexes should return and then become brisk.

**When.** The illness has evolved over hours to days, starting ten days after an infection, with back pain at the onset.

**What.** Here the order of the list matters more than its contents. A compressing epidural abscess, hematoma or tumor is less likely than inflammation. It is, however, the diagnosis that delay makes permanent, so urgent imaging excludes it first. Transverse myelitis fits the tempo and the preceding infection. The clue many would miss is last week's blurred vision, which together with an afferent pupillary defect suggests optic neuritis. Optic neuritis with myelitis points toward MOG antibody disease or neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, the first being the more common in children, and that changes both the testing and the treatment.

**The trap.** The first trap is imaging only at the level found on the skin. The sensory level can sit several segments below the actual lesion, especially with lesions outside the cord (Brazis 2011, p. 104). A T10 level on the skin therefore does not mean a T10 lesion, and the whole spine needs imaging. The second trap is Guillain-Barré syndrome, which is easy to suspect when weak legs and reduced reflexes follow an infection. Guillain-Barré rarely produces a sensory level or early retention, and it does not cause upgoing toes.

Where, when, what: "Spinal cord, acute over a day after an infection, with recent optic neuritis, so compression is excluded first and then transverse myelitis is pursued with antibody testing for neuromyelitis optica spectrum and MOG antibody disease."
keyPoints: A sensory level on the trunk almost always comes from the cord, and early retention agrees (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
Reduced reflexes in an acute cord lesion reflect spinal shock, while upgoing toes still show the upper motor neuron (DeMyer, pp. 273-274).
The sensory level on the skin can lie several segments below the lesion, so image the whole spine (Brazis 2011, p. 104).
Exclude compression first, and remember that optic neuritis plus myelitis points to antibody-mediated disease.

question.question: Her sensory level is at T10. The radiographer asks whether imaging only the lower thoracic spine will do. What do you answer?
options: Yes, because the lesion is at T10
Image only the lumbar spine, because the legs are weak
No, image the whole spine (and the brain, given the optic neuritis), because the true lesion can lie several segments above the level on the skin
No imaging is needed until the cerebrospinal fluid results return
question.explanation: The sensory level on the trunk shows where the sensory loss begins, which is not necessarily where the lesion is, and with some lesions it sits many segments below the real level. Imaging only around T10 risks missing a higher lesion, and the recent optic neuritis makes brain imaging part of the same question. Imaging only the lumbar spine looks entirely below the level. Delaying imaging for the cerebrospinal fluid results is dangerous, because compression has to be excluded first and a lumbar puncture does not exclude it.

sections.title: Case 5: a 3-year-old who suddenly cannot walk straight
sections.content:
**Where.** Ataxia counts as cerebellar only once weakness and sensory loss have been excluded, because both can make a child unsteady. In this boy strength, reflexes and the plantar responses are normal. His unsteadiness therefore reflects a failure of coordination in the cerebellum or its connections. A wide-based, staggering gait with only mild overshoot of the limbs points to the midline, because disorders of the midline cerebellum affect the trunk and balance most (Brazis 2011, p. 411).

**When.** He became ataxic overnight, ten days after a viral illness with a rash.

**What.** Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia is the commonest cause in a well, alert young child, and it is the diagnosis here. The list still has to carry two others. A toxic ingestion belongs on the list for any toddler with acute ataxia, however carefully the house was checked. Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia can begin with ataxia alone, before the chaotic eye movements, the jerks and the irritability appear. It matters because it sends you looking for a neuroblastoma.

**The trap.** It is easy to order imaging, or to offer reassurance, by reflex rather than by reading the clock. A posterior fossa tumor is the fear behind every ataxic child, but tumors evolve over weeks, usually with headache, morning vomiting or papilledema. An overnight onset in a cheerful child with sharp discs fits poorly, and what should change your mind is ataxia that persists or worsens. The second trap is examining the eyes only once. Opsoclonus may be absent on the first day, so plan a second look in a few days with that question in mind.

Where, when, what: "Cerebellum, midline, acute overnight after a viral illness, most likely post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia, with ingestion screened and a review planned to look for opsoclonus and myoclonus."
keyPoints: Ataxia is cerebellar only once weakness and sensory loss have been excluded.
Midline cerebellar disease affects the trunk and balance most, and hemispheric disease affects the limbs on the same side (Brazis 2011, p. 411).
In a toddler with acute ataxia, think of post-infectious ataxia first, consider an ingestion every time, and watch for opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.
Tumors evolve over weeks, so an overnight onset with a normal fundus fits poorly, although persistence or worsening calls for imaging.

question.question: Five days later the same boy is more irritable, has jerks of his arms, and his eyes make rapid, chaotic movements in all directions. What should happen next?
options: Continue observation, because post-infectious ataxia takes weeks to resolve
Treat the new findings as opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia and search for a neuroblastoma
Send a toxicology screen, because the new movements suggest an ingestion
Arrange nerve conduction studies
question.explanation: Chaotic, multidirectional eye movements, myoclonic jerks and irritability added to ataxia make up the picture of opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia, which can begin as ataxia alone. It calls for a search for a neuroblastoma and for specialist treatment. Post-infectious ataxia improves over time and does not produce opsoclonus, so continued observation would miss the change. An ingestion would not explain a new syndrome emerging five days into a stable illness, and nerve conduction studies examine the peripheral nervous system, which is not where this problem lies.

sections.title: Case 6: a 7-year-old who sees double when looking to one side
sections.content:
**Where.** Start with the sign that brought her in, because it is the one most likely to mislead. A weak lateral rectus invites you to the sixth-nerve nucleus in the pons, or to the nerve somewhere along its route. But the sixth nerve has a long course, and it is among the first to suffer when the pressure inside the skull rises. The cause may be a tumor above or below the tentorium, hydrocephalus or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Pearl 2014, p. 43). In raised pressure the palsy is a nonlocalizing sign (Pearl 2014, p. 48), and with papilledema it is the commonest of the **false localizing signs** (Brazis 2011, p. 622). It is better read as a report that the pressure is high than as a marker of where the lesion sits.

To find the address, look at the company the palsy keeps. Swollen discs say the pressure is high, and a wide-based, staggering gait with only mild overshoot of the limbs is the midline cerebellar pattern (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A normal face and swallow argue against an intrinsic pontine lesion. The facial nerve loops around the sixth-nerve nucleus (Pearl 2014, p. 48), and damage at the nucleus tends to produce a gaze palsy rather than one weak eye (Pearl 2014, p. 43).

**When.** Over several weeks the headache came first, then the double vision, then the unsteadiness. Each symptom was added to the last, which is how a growing lesion tends to behave.

**What.** A single midline mass in the posterior fossa explains everything at once. It unsettles the trunk and compresses the fourth ventricle, and the trapped fluid raises the pressure (Arslan 2014, p. 98). The raised pressure in turn swells the discs and stretches the sixth nerve. Posterior fossa tumors are common in children, with medulloblastoma and cystic (pilocytic) astrocytoma among them, and ependymoma is the third to keep in mind (Pearl 2014, p. 63).

**The prior.** Examined alone, a sixth-nerve palsy has a long list of possible sites and causes along its whole route (Brazis 2011, p. 202), and a clinician who looked only at the eyes could defend almost any of them. The fundi change the question before a single test is ordered. Once the discs are swollen, every hypothesis that cannot raise the pressure falls away, and the scan becomes a confirmation rather than a search. A test acts as an opinion modifier on a prior ([Gill 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15879401/)), and in this case the ophthalmoscope set the prior without costing anything.

**The trap.** The first trap is skipping the fundi in a child with headache because a fidgety child is hard to examine. The fundi are the one examination here that changes the plan. The second is the lumbar puncture, since a suspected posterior fossa mass is a reason to image before any needle (DeMyer, pp. 545-546).

Where, when, what: "Posterior fossa, midline cerebellum, with raised pressure, subacute over weeks, most likely a tumor with obstructive hydrocephalus and the sixth-nerve palsy a false localizing sign, needing urgent imaging and neurosurgery."
keyPoints: A sixth-nerve palsy is an early, nonlocalizing sign of raised pressure from many causes (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 48; Brazis 2011, p. 622).
The address comes from the company the palsy keeps, and papilledema with a wide-based gait points to a midline posterior fossa mass (Brazis 2011, p. 412).
The fundi set the prior, because once the discs are swollen the sixth nerve needs no address of its own.
When a posterior fossa mass is suspected, image before any lumbar puncture (DeMyer, pp. 545-546).

question.question: A 9-year-old boy has had two weeks of morning headaches and now sees double when he looks to the right; his right eye does not move fully outward. The clinic is running late and you have not yet looked at his fundi. What do you do next?
options: Refer him to orthoptics for a squint assessment, since the problem is in the eye
Request imaging aimed at the pons, where the sixth-nerve nucleus lies
Reassure the family and review him in a month
Examine his fundi now, because swollen discs would turn the palsy into a sign of raised pressure and change the urgency
question.explanation: On its own, a sixth-nerve palsy cannot tell you where the problem is, because its long course leaves it vulnerable to raised pressure from many causes (Pearl 2014, p. 43). The fundi decide what the palsy means. Swollen discs make it a false localizing sign and make imaging urgent, while normal discs reopen the local causes along the nerve. Imaging aimed at the pons would look for a local lesion when the palsy may only be reporting raised pressure. A squint referral or a month's wait would leave raised pressure unrecognized if it is there, and morning headaches with a new palsy are no reason to wait.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old woke with weakness of the right face, arm and leg and cannot find his words. His reflexes are brisk on the right. Where is the lesion?
options: Left cerebral hemisphere, cortex
Right cerebral hemisphere
Spinal cord
Left pons
quiz.explanation: Weakness of the face, arm and leg on the same side places the lesion above the facial nucleus, and difficulty finding words is a cortical sign of the dominant hemisphere, which for most children is the left. Because the corticospinal tract crosses, right-sided weakness means a lesion in the left hemisphere. The cord cannot weaken the face or cause aphasia. A pontine lesion would usually give a crossed pattern, with a cranial nerve affected on one side and the body on the other, and would not cause aphasia.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old's eyelids droop by the evening, and her voice fades as she talks. Her reflexes and sensation are normal. Where is the problem?
options: Muscle
Brainstem
Peripheral nerve
Neuromuscular junction
quiz.explanation: Weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest, in the eyelids and the voice, is fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness, the signature of the neuromuscular junction, as in juvenile myasthenia gravis. A myopathy can cause ptosis but does not usually fluctuate this way. A brainstem lesion causes fixed rather than fatigable deficits, usually with other signs, and a peripheral nerve lesion would reduce the reflexes or cause sensory loss, both of which are normal here.

quiz.question: An alert 4-month-old is floppy, with absent reflexes and fine fasciculations of the tongue. She has no sensory abnormality you can detect. Which level fits best?
options: Muscle
Anterior horn cell
Cerebral cortex
Neuromuscular junction
quiz.explanation: An alert, floppy infant with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations has denervated muscle, and a purely motor picture with fasciculations points to the anterior horn cell, as in spinal muscular atrophy. Primary muscle disease does not fasciculate. Cortical hypotonia comes with depressed alertness and normal or brisk reflexes. Disease of the junction does not cause fasciculations, and the reflexes are usually preserved.

quiz.question: A 12-year-old has a left sixth-nerve palsy and a weak right arm and leg. Where is the lesion?
options: Left medial pons
Right medial pons
Left internal capsule
Right cerebral cortex
quiz.explanation: A cranial nerve sign on one side with weakness of the body on the other is a crossed pattern, which only the brainstem can produce, and the cranial nerve marks the side and level of the lesion. The fibers of the sixth nerve run forward through the medial pons, past the corticospinal tract before that tract has crossed. A left ventral medial pontine lesion therefore gives a left sixth-nerve palsy and a right hemiparesis (Brazis 2011, p. 202). A right pontine lesion would give a right sixth-nerve palsy, and capsular and cortical lesions do not cause a sixth-nerve palsy at all.

quiz.question: An 8-year-old developed foot drop after weeks of sitting cross-legged during a long hospital stay. Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion are weak; inversion and hip abduction are normal; the ankle reflex is present. Where is the lesion?
options: L5 root
Sciatic nerve
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
Spinal cord
quiz.explanation: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with normal inversion and hip abduction separate a common peroneal nerve lesion from an L5 root lesion. Inversion, through the tibial nerve, and hip abduction, through the superior gluteal nerve, share the L5 root but not the peroneal nerve, so both would be weak in an L5 radiculopathy (Morris 2012, p. 26). Sitting cross-legged compresses the peroneal nerve at the fibular head. A sciatic lesion would weaken inversion through the tibial branch, and a cord lesion would bring upper motor neuron signs and usually affect both legs.

quiz.question: A 6-year-old boy has had three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. Both optic discs are swollen, his left eye does not abduct fully, and he walks on a wide base while his finger-nose testing is nearly normal. His mother asks whether a lumbar puncture would be quicker than a scan. What do you advise?
options: A lumbar puncture first, to measure the opening pressure
A lumbar puncture first, because a sixth-nerve palsy with papilledema means idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Neither yet, and refer to ophthalmology for the double vision
Brain imaging first, because a posterior fossa mass is likely and a lumbar puncture could precipitate herniation
quiz.explanation: Papilledema with a wide-based gait and little limb ataxia points to a midline posterior fossa mass raising the pressure, and the sixth-nerve palsy is a false localizing sign of that pressure (Brazis 2011, pp. 412, 622). A suspected posterior fossa mass is a reason to image before any lumbar puncture (DeMyer, pp. 545-546), so the pressure should not be measured first. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension can cause the same eye signs, but it is raised pressure without a mass (Arslan 2014, p. 191), which means it can only be diagnosed after imaging. An eye referral would only delay the scan.

signOff: The resident completes all six cases and presents one of them, or a real patient, to faculty in where, when, what form.

opener.parable: Each case that follows asks you to commit at every step, to a level, a time course and a short list, before anything is revealed. Committing feels risky, but a localization you can revise will teach you far more than a list of possibilities you never had to defend.
opener.history: Georges Guillain (1876–1961) and J. A. Barré (1880–1967), French neurologists, gave their names to the paralysis in the first case, in which weakness climbs, the reflexes disappear and a child stops walking.
